inputs.original_text: This looks less like a spontaneous response and more like a carefully managed political spectacle. Hundreds of groups were involved, and holding the rally weeks before local elections gives the timing a purpose: keep the far-right threat front and centre and steer what voters are allowed to focus on. The “stand against extremism” framing may be the cover; mass rallies can also signal which views are acceptable and funnel public opinion where the organisers want it. I wouldn’t assume this was organic.
inputs.modified_text: The rally’s scale and its timing weeks before local elections make the “spontaneous” story hard to swallow. Hundreds of groups don’t simply converge around a message by accident; this looks coordinated to keep voters focused on a designated far-right threat while narrowing the range of views treated as acceptable. The anti-extremism language may be less a warning than a tool for steering public opinion. The real question is who benefits from directing attention this way—and what they don’t want voters looking at instead.
